claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin native oxide layer.
The native oxide film on Q235 steel is initially a relatively dense and adherent layer.
The initial native oxide film is dominated by magnetite (Fe3O4).
At room temperature, the native oxide limits corrosion by restricting oxygen and ion diffusion.
Aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C transforms the initial oxide into a more porous and less adherent scale.
The high-temperature oxide transformation may involve conversion of magnetite to hematite (Fe2O3).
High-temperature exposure increases oxide-scale porosity.
Thermal-mechanical stresses generated at high temperature cause oxide-scale spallation.
Oxide-scale spallation exposes fresh Q235 steel to corrosive salts.
Exposure of fresh metal following scale disruption accelerates corrosive attack.
Relative to room-temperature exposure, aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C will produce a marked increase in mass change.
The high-temperature mass change will reflect both oxide-scale growth and spallation.
High-temperature samples will exhibit more extensive oxide-scale disruption than room-temperature samples.
High-temperature samples will exhibit deeper corrosion penetration than room-temperature samples.
The high-temperature scale will contain a mixture enriched in, or predominated by, Fe2O3 relative to the lower-temperature scale.
Room-temperature Q235 coupons retain limited but stable corrosion protection without significant oxide transformation or spallation.
Pre-treatment that forms a stable protective scale would prevent the proposed mechanism from applying.
The oxide transformation and critical disruption temperature depend on minor composition variations and exposure duration.
XRD, SEM/EDS, mass-change measurements, and cross-sectional microscopy can test the predicted oxide-phase, morphology, and corrosion-penetration differences.
Failure to observe either the proposed high-temperature oxide disruption or a significant corrosion difference from the room-temperature baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
